intrinsic_value_estimate: About $55–65 per share. Method: 1988 owner earnings of about $2.30–2.70 per share (net income plus depreciation and non-cash items, minus undistributed equity income, minus capex), grown 12% a year for 10 years, then 5% a year forever, discounted at the company's stated 12% after-tax cost of capital, plus about $2.50 per share of affiliate stakes net of debt. The range is $49 at 8% growth and $80 at 15% growth. At a 10% discount rate the value is $69–93. The packet has no long-bond yield, so the discount rate is my assumption.
margin_of_safety: Price $46.56 against central value $55–65 gives a margin of about 18–28%. In the conservative case (8% growth, 12% discount rate) the margin is about 5%. The price passes the framework's standard of a price that makes sense even if the future looks like the past, but it is not a deep-discount bargain. Protection comes mainly from the quality of the business. If the price fell back toward the 1988 range of $35–39, the margin would widen to about 35–45%.

key_reasons.reason: High returns on equity for a long time, with modest net leverage: the primary test of business and management quality.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: ROE from continuing operations was 19.4–21.2% every year 1977–83, then 23.5% (1985), 28.8% (1986, about 24.6% excluding one-offs), 27.2% (1987) and 33% (1988, upi-1989-01-31). Net debt was 15.3% of capital at end-1987 (ar-1987). Equity investments returned only about 5%, which implies the concentrate business earns far higher returns on its own capital.

key_reasons.reason: A wide brand-and-distribution moat that management keeps widening, like GEICO's.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Durable competitive advantage: the moat around the castle (brk-letter-1986#16)
key_reasons.evidence: U.S. share above 40% in 1988, up from 39% in 1986. 59% of U.S. fountain, more than 2-to-1 over the nearest rival. 44% of soft drinks sold worldwide, double the nearest competitor's volume. Restated operating margin rose from 13.7% to 15.4% to 17.8% (1985–87, excluding provisions). Concentrate gross margin about 63% (ar-1986). Per-capita consumption outside the U.S. is 16% of the U.S. rate.

key_reasons.reason: Owner earnings are large and growing because the core business needs little capital.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Owner earnings (brk-letter-1986); low capital needs (brk-letter-1987#1, fortune-1977-inflation)
key_reasons.evidence: 1987 working capital from operations $958.8M against capex of $299.6M, so owner earnings were about $660–810M ($1.75–2.15 per share). On the conservative definition they rose from about $359M in 1985 to $659M in 1987. Cash from operations of $1.23B covered capex about four times (ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: Retained earnings have produced far more than $1 of market value per $1, and buybacks are demonstrated, not just announced.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value (brk-letter-1983); buybacks below value (brk-letter-1984#4)
key_reasons.evidence: About $2.3–2.6B retained in 1982–88 against about $13B of value created (market value from $4.3B to about $15.8B, plus about $2.2B returned through buybacks), or about $2.7 per $1 even with the P/E held constant. About 69M shares repurchased since 1984. The 40M-share program is 25.5M complete (upi-1989-01-31).

key_reasons.reason: Price is sensible for an outstanding business: an owner-earnings yield of about 5.4% plus growth of 10–13% implies returns of about 11–17% a year with no re-rating needed.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Outstanding business at a sensible price, not a mediocre one at a bargain (brk-letter-1987#18; brk-letter-1979; brk-letter-1981#3). The §5 net-working-capital rule is superseded for franchises.
key_reasons.evidence: $46.56 is 16.3x 1988 EPS of $2.85. Net income compounded about 13.4% a year from 1981 ($432M) to 1988 ($1,040M). Net working capital is only about $0.05 per share, so the old bargain test does not apply.

key_reasons.reason: The facts are clear and the franchise is hard to damage, so a concentrated position is justified. Size is held below the maximum because the margin is moderate.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §7 Concentrate when the facts are clear (bpl-letter-1965)
key_reasons.evidence: EPS rose every year from 1977 to 1988. Simple concentrate business with no technology risk. Market value about $16.5B and very liquid (NYSE, Dow component), so a position large enough to matter to Berkshire can be built.

key_reasons.reason: No catalyst needed; hold indefinitely as a general position.
key_reasons.evidence: No pending sale, merger or tender. Returns come from compounding owner earnings. The ongoing buyback raises a holder's ownership percentage over time.

risks: Managers who diversified into entertainment and Foods in 1982–86 now have about $1.2B of borrowing capacity (35% net-debt ceiling) and could again spend franchise cash outside the core.

Leverage is drifting upward: short-term debt rose about $1.2B in 1987, partly to fund buybacks near the year's high. CCE carries $2.72B of liabilities. Company A has about $394M of contingent guarantees plus $325M of guaranteed CPE receivables.
Currency: about 74–77% of operating income comes from outside the U.S. Key currencies strengthened 27%, 16% and 10% in 1986–88, and that translation boost could reverse.
Low returns on capital in the equity affiliates (CCE about 6%, CPE write-downs in 1988) and a commodity-like Foods unit (frozen orange juice volume down 22% in 1988) dilute the core returns.
U.S. formula pricing with most non-CCE bottlers limits pricing power on the flagship product at home.
Price is near the 52-week high of $49.12 after a re-rating from about 10x to 16x earnings since 1981. The margin of safety is thin in the conservative case.
The annual reports' narrative is promotional (the 1986 entertainment and Foods outlooks were reversed within a year). Character and integrity cannot be checked from the packet.
what_would_change_my_mind: Meeting management shows they are not owner-oriented, or the proxy shows heavy pay disconnected from per-share value and small insider holdings.
The 1988 annual report shows owner earnings well below about $2.30 per share, or capex needed just to hold position running far above depreciation.
A long-term government bond yield high enough (around 10% or more) that a 5.4% owner-earnings yield plus growth no longer beats the risk-free alternative.
Evidence that the primary competitor is closing the share gap, or that concentrate pricing has not kept pace with inflation.
A large new acquisition outside soft drinks, or stock issued on terms below intrinsic value.
A drop in price toward $35–39 with the business unchanged would raise conviction and justify buying more.
sell_triggers: The fundamental economics were misread: sustained loss of U.S. or worldwide share, or operating margins in soft drinks reversing for reasons other than currency (brk-letter-1987#18 notes a marketable holding is easier to exit than a controlled one).
Management shows insensitivity to owners: issuing shares below value, or moving large amounts of capital into non-core businesses earning below the 12% hurdle (brk-letter-1982#17).
Leverage pushed well beyond the stated 35% net-debt ceiling to fund financial engineering rather than the business.
Evidence that management is dishonest or that reported numbers are materially misleading.
A high price alone is NOT a trigger. Under the framework's default (§8) a great business with good managers is held indefinitely.
